title: Choose the dashboard layout
question: Three ways to run today’s route. Same navy / sand / citrus, same live bookings. Lock one.

options.label: Window board
options.lineage: Hotel dispatch sheet grouped by delivery window
options.thesis: Today’s stops read as a departure board: morning, afternoon, then flexible — hotel name first, In or Out on every row.
options.viewport: Date and giant In/Out counts head the page. Three window bands of hotel-first rows fill the fold. Remaining scooters this week and pending payments sit under the route.
options.risk: Staff who think in hotel order, not time of day, have to scan three bands to find one stop.

raised.raise: Stops are time-ranked rows; status restyles the row without breaking the grid.
In and Out counts are the only oversized type — live tiles of the day’s load.

options.label: Two docks
options.thesis: Deliveries and pickups sit as equal columns you work down, hotel and guest first, window as a quiet tag.
options.viewport: A short today header, then two equal docks of stop cards. Remaining units as a strip under both columns. Pending pay as a slim row. Stacks to Deliveries then Pickups on a phone.
options.risk: On a phone, pickups wait below a long delivery list.

options.label: Catch then go
options.lineage: Exception tickets above the day’s route
options.thesis: Pending payments and sold-out days sit as a short ticket strip, then today’s In and Out lists so problems do not hide under the route.
options.viewport: Exception tickets across the top. Today’s deliveries and pickups as two lists. Inventory last. Quiet days show an empty-ticket line, not a blank page.
options.risk: Quiet days put an empty problem strip above the work, which can feel like a false alarm.
